items.bodyEn: Okitsu grew up beside the Kiyomi barrier, an ancient checkpoint where mountains pinch the coast road against the sea. The eleventh-century Sarashina Diary describes its guardhouses and a palisade reaching the water. The Zen temple Seikenji stands on the site and lodged Korean embassies in the Edo period. Hiroshige shows two sumo wrestlers being carried across the Okitsu River.
items.sourceNote: Sarashina Nikki (c. 1060); Hiroshige, 'Okitsu: Okitsu River' (Hōeidō ed.)

items.bodyEn: The kanji for kuru began as a picture of a wheat plant, ears drooping. The ancient Chinese dictionary Shuowen explains that wheat was 'sent from heaven', so the sign was borrowed for the verb 'to come', and the grain later got its own character. Every てくる you say this week rides on a borrowed ear of wheat.
items.sourceNote: Shuowen Jiezi (c. 100 CE), entry 來; standard kanji etymologies

items.bodyEn: After a dictionary form, な forbids: いくな, 'don't go'. After the ます-stem, な is a clipped なさい and gently commands: いきな, 'go on, then'. One syllable apart, opposite meanings, so listen for the verb ending. Both are blunt and belong to parents, coaches and close friends; with anyone else, fall back on 〜てください or 〜ないでください.

Anzuru yori umu ga yasushi: giving birth is easier than worrying about it. Said to someone frozen by what might go wrong, it means the doing is usually lighter than the dread. It pairs naturally with 〜てみる: stop fretting and try it. Yasushi is the classical form of yasashii, 'easy', the ending you will meet again in old sayings.
items.ja: {案|あん}ずるより{産|う}むが{易|やす}し。
items.kana: あんずるよりうむがやすし。
